name: Standard Scramble (South/East Slopes)
beta: From the Heather Meadows/Bagley Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Bagley Lakes Trail up toward Herman Saddle, then leave the trail near the last switchback to gain the ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman. From there the route generally follows the south/southwest ridge to the summit over a mix of dirt, talus, and short class 3 rock steps; in early season the ridge and gullies hold snow and are often climbed with an ice axe and crampons, or skied/split-boarded as a ski-mountaineering tour. It is also frequently combined with a loop past Chain Lakes.
overview: An off-trail scramble above Heather Meadows on the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) — despite easy road access it is climbed far less often than neighbors like Table Mountain or Church Mountain, and is best known locally among backcountry skiers who ski/ride its couloirs. From the Bagley Lakes/Chain Lakes Trail near Herman Saddle, parties leave the maintained trail and pick a line up heather benches and scree to the south ridge, finishing on a short, loose, exposed east ridge to a summit with a 1939 USGS survey marker and views of Mount Baker, Mount Shuksan, the Pickets, and the border peaks (Larrabee, American Border Peak, Tomyhoi).

current.approach: Start from the Bagley Lakes Trailhead (~4,200 ft) at the south end of the upper Mt. Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 684.1) south along the eastern shore of Bagley Lake — this is the only reliable water source on the route, and it should still be filtered/treated. At about 0.75 mile, the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 682), which bends west and begins switchbacking up toward Herman Saddle (~5,300 ft), roughly 1.5-2 miles and about 1,100 ft above the lakes. Snow frequently lingers on this slope into July or even August, and the Forest Service explicitly flags it as avalanche terrain in winter/spring conditions, so check current conditions before an early-season trip; poles and some route-finding are recommended even on the maintained tread. At the last switchback below Herman Saddle — the low point on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome (west) and Mount Herman (east) — leave the maintained trail and go cross-country, climbing open heather slopes and a short band of scrub trees for a couple hundred vertical feet to gain the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge. This off-trail stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach; the correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility. Once on the ridge, follow its crest generally eastward, staying mostly on the south/southwest side over heather benches and loose scree/talus, to the base of a short final east ridge that leads to the true summit at 6,285 ft.
approach_variant_names: Bagley Lakes and Chain Lakes Trail to the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then cross-country to the ridge
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent descent route. Downclimb the short summit east ridge back to the south/southwest ridge, then follow that ridge and its heather-and-scree slopes back down to the low saddle point between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman. Drop off the ridge on the same cross-country line through the scrub-tree band and heather slopes to rejoin the maintained Chain Lakes Trail (682) at the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then follow Chain Lakes Trail and Bagley Lakes Trail (684.1) back past Bagley Lakes to the trailhead. This is a walk-off scramble with no rappelling required under normal summer/dry conditions — 0 rappels. The main descent hazards are loose, down-sloping scree and talus on the ridge and connecting slopes (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below), and lingering snow in the gully/ridge-traverse sections in early season, where an ice axe and/or microspikes are a reasonable precaution; a rope is not standard gear for this route.
current.rope_note: South/East Slopes standard scramble via Herman Saddle; Class 2-3 ridge/snow travel. Rope not standard; aluminum crampons/ice axe useful in shoulder-season snow.

name: Hinman Glacier / Standard
beta: Most climbers approach from Necklace Valley (9 miles, 5,100 ft gain), the shortest and most common route. The ascent involves 4-9 miles of off-trail scrambling from La Bohn Lakes, gaining 2,500-3,000 ft to the summit via Class 2 talus and snow slopes. The Hinman Glacier (namesake feature) has largely disappeared as of August 2022, leaving only stranded patches of snow/ice. Standard gear includes ice axe, crampons, GPS, and map. Most climbers execute this as a 2-3 day backpacking trip.
overview: Mount Hinman is a broad glaciated dome neighboring Mount Daniel (7,960 ft, less than 2 miles east). First climbed in 1928 and named in 1934 for Dr. Harry B. Hinman, a founding member of an Everett climbing club, the peak once carried two glaciers — Hinman Glacier on its north flank and the smaller Foss Glacier to the northeast — but Hinman Glacier was declared dead (no longer flowing) by 2022, and both are now reduced to stagnant, shrinking ice/snow patches. The standard route climbs from La Bohn Gap up the peak's north side, crossing the former glacier basins on now largely bare, unstable talus rather than true glacier ice.

current.approach: Park at the Necklace Valley Trailhead (~1,650 ft) at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are deceptively easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail follows the East Fork Foss River through regenerated second-growth forest (logged in the 1930s), entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness at about 1.5 miles. Around the 5-mile mark the trail crosses the East Fork Foss River on a footlog with a handwire (the river runs high and cold under it in early-season snowmelt, so plan the crossing for morning low flow) and then turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 2,400 ft over the next 3 miles on steep, root-laced switchbacks into Necklace Valley proper. This section is the approach's real crux for tired legs and pack weight. The trail eases again as it reaches Jade Lake (~4,600 ft, ~8-9 miles), then Emerald Lake a quarter mile beyond, then Opal Lake, threading through the swampy, lake-studded Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water throughout, but buggy in early/mid-summer. From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends; continue cross-country (an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus) up and southeast roughly 1-1.5 miles and ~1,000+ ft to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes, the standard high camp for the peak (total approach to La Bohn Gap is about 10-11 miles one-way with ~5,000+ ft of cumulative gain). From La Bohn Gap the route continues north-northeast into what remains of the Hinman/Foss Glacier basin — now much diminished and largely bare rock/permanent snowfield rather than a true crevassed glacier in most recent seasons, but still worth crampons/axe and glacier-travel judgment in early season or after a big snow year — then east/east-northeast via easy class 2 ridge/scree scrambling to the summit ridge and along it about half a mile to the true summit (7,492 ft). Loose rock on the final scramble and potential crevasse/bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant (mostly early-season) are the main approach-specific risks beyond the river crossing and the steep valley headwall.
approach_variant_names: Necklace Valley to La Bohn Gap and the lakes
current.descent: This is a walk-off / downclimb descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line the entire way. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ridge scramble back to the top of the glacier remnant, descend the snow/glacier basin back to La Bohn Gap (watch for softened, sun-cupped snow and any residual crevasse slots in early season), then follow the cairned climbers' path back down through the talus and meadow to La Bohn Lakes/Necklace Basin. Most parties treat this as a multi-day trip (roundtrip totals run 22-26 miles with 5,700-9,000 ft of cumulative gain/loss depending on exact line), descending from the summit back to a La Bohn Lakes or Necklace Basin camp the same day and hiking the remaining ~9-10 miles out to the trailhead — back down through Necklace Basin past Opal, Emerald, and Jade Lakes, down the steep rooty 2,400-ft headwall, back across the East Fork Foss River footlog, and out the long, gentle lower trail — on a subsequent day. No technical rope work is required on the standard route; the notable descent hazards are the same river crossing, loose talus, and glacier-remnant travel encountered on the way in, now tackled with tired legs late in the day.
current.detailed_rack: Roped glacier travel is no longer typically needed now that Hinman Glacier has stopped flowing, though conditions (and thus gear needs) can vary year to year -- check recent trip reports.
current.pro_needs: Minimal; snow/glacier protection.
bivy: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead

name: Standard Scramble
beta: This is not a technical climb but a serious backcountry scramble: about 13.1 trail miles from the Staircase trailhead to First Divide/Home Sweet Home camp, then off-trail travel east over talus, heather benches, and a short rocky ridge to the summit. Most parties backpack in and camp at Home Sweet Home (just below First Divide) to split the approach over two days. The Staircase trail, the Home Sweet Home Trail and the camps along them are currently closed after the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, so check the park's trail status first. A shorter but steeper off-trail alternative climbs from Lake of the Angels (reached via the Putvin Trail), crossing the ridge and dropping into the valley below Mount Stone before climbing the ridge west of Stone toward Hopper.
overview: Mount Hopper (6,120 ft) is a deep-interior Olympic summit in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, on the Skokomish–Duckabush divide near First Divide. Its line parent is Mount Steel (6,612 ft), about 1.96 miles west-northwest; Mount Duckabush, Mount LaCrosse, and White Mountain are also nearby. The peak is named for brothers Stanley and Roland Hopper, sons of a Singer Sewing Machine Company executive — Stanley took part in W. G. Steel's 1906 ascent of neighboring Mount Steel. The standard Class 2 line is straightforward climbing, but the historically standard Staircase/North Fork Skokomish approach has been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, and so has the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide that the longer Duckabush River Trail alternative needs, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026.

current.approach: The North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date; check the park's trail conditions before planning. When open, the standard way in starts at the Staircase trailhead (~785 ft) and follows the North Fork Skokomish River Trail up the valley through old-growth forest, past Camp Pleasant to Nine Stream Camp, where the trail fords the river (deep and swift in high snowmelt or heavy rain). Above Nine Stream it climbs steeply past Two Bear Camp, brushy between Two Bear and the divide, to First Divide (4,688 ft), about 12.5 miles from the trailhead. The much longer alternative comes up the Duckabush River Trail and climbs over First Divide from the north past Home Sweet Home. Just below First Divide on the Skokomish side, the long-abandoned Mount Hopper Way leaves the main trail; its tread has gone under brush, so expect to bushwhack south and east through forest, then climb open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Most parties make it a multi-day trip, camping at Two Bear Camp, First Divide or Home Sweet Home rather than pushing car-to-car.
approach_variant_names: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the same gully/rib system off the summit rockwall back down through the steepest rock step, then the easier talus and heather below it, back to the basin and First Divide (4,688 ft). This is a scramble route with no fixed anchors or bolted stations reported anywhere on it — the standard descent is careful downclimbing, facing in through the steeper rocky steps near the top where the wall lays back into a short climbable face. Some parties uncomfortable reversing that headwall step opt for a single, short rappel off a natural anchor (slung horn or block — bring webbing/cord, since none is fixed in place) to protect the crux; this is optional, not required, so plan on 0 fixed rappels for a typical descent. Watch for loose rock and rockfall onto any party below in the gully system, and re-identify your ascent gully carefully from above — the same routefinding hazard (many similar-looking gullies and ribs) applies in reverse and is arguably worse on the way down. From First Divide, reverse the North Fork Skokomish Trail about 12.5 miles to Staircase (or, if you came in from the Duckabush, drop past Home Sweet Home to the Duckabush River Trail and walk it out). Both trails off First Divide, the Home Sweet Home Trail toward the Duckabush and the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase, are currently closed after the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire; check the park's trail status before planning.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard class 2 route — it is unroped scrambling on talus, heather, and a short rocky ridge.
current.pro_needs: No technical pro; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow on the approach slopes.
bivy: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
current.rope_note: Class 2 approach via First Divide/North Fork Skokomish or Lake of the Angels ridge; steep snow sections early season warrant ice axe, but route is not roped.

name: South Slope
beta: Most parties reach Crescent Lake, which sits below Howard's south side along the Nason Ridge Trail, from either the Merritt Lake Trailhead (shorter, more direct) or the Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock-Crescent col (longer, more scenic, and commonly combined with Rock Mountain). From Crescent Lake's NE side, ascend north up open talus and meadow slopes; the upper mountain narrows into a loose, dirty class 3 gully before easing back to talus and a climbers' trail to the summit. Many parties combine the ascent with a traverse to neighboring Mount Mastiff (about 1 mile away) or Rock Mountain for a full Nason Ridge outing.
overview: The standard and easiest line to Mount Howard's summit: a long off-trail approach via the Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake, followed by a Class 2-3 scramble up the peak's broad, open south-facing slope and a short loose gully to the summit ridge.

current.approach: Two common trailheads on US-2 in Chelan County give access. Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,000 ft, high-clearance/AWD recommended on the access road): from Leavenworth take US-2 west about 24 miles (or from Stevens Pass, east about 11.5 miles) to milepost 76, turn onto Forest Road 657, and continue 1.5 miles to the trailhead; hike the Merritt Lake Trail (2,000 ft gain in 2.5 miles) then join the Nason Ridge Trail east to Crescent Lake. Rock Mountain Trailhead (2,650-2,675 ft, no fee): on US-2 near milepost 73, about 27 miles west of Leavenworth / 8.5 miles east of Stevens Pass; follow the Rock Mountain Trail up to Rock Lake (snow persists above ~5,000 ft into late spring), then over the Rock-Crescent col and down about 500 ft to Crescent Lake. From either approach, water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain.
approach_variant_names: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
current.descent: Downclimb the loose class 3 gully on the upper south face with care — it is dirty and holds are unreliable in both directions. Below that, descend talus and open slopes back to Crescent Lake. In early-season (spring) conditions the col/gully snow can refreeze firm overnight, making crampons and an ice axe useful for a controlled descent; some parties glissade snow-filled sections when soft. From Crescent Lake, retrace the Nason Ridge Trail to the trailhead, watching for the correct drainage — parties have mistakenly dropped toward Royal Creek from the ridge.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard south-slope scramble in summer conditions — it is a talus/gully scramble up to loose class 3.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used — this is an unroped Class 2/2+ scramble with no roped pitches.
bivy: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps

name: Bluebell
beta: Seventeen pitches as usually linked (21 if split at every stance), in six sections: the Toe (P1-3); the slightly overhanging Shield (P4-6) with the 3D Dike and a boulder-problem crux on blank pinches; the steep Roofs (P7-8); the technical Slab (P9-11), with a ledge at P10 that takes a portaledge; the overhanging Headwall (P12-15) with the 5.13- crux; and easier, barely cleaned Summit pitches (P16-17). Bring a stick clip for the headwall bolts.
overview: Bluebell is the first free route up the North Norwegian Buttress of Mount Index: about 2,000 ft of climbing graded 5.13-, protected entirely by bolts, with roughly a third of its pitches overhanging. Most of it is sustained 5.11-5.12. It is its own line, independent of the Doorish, Voodoo Project and Jötnar aid routes, and it took more than 25 days on the wall to establish in 2023.

current.approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead (~600 ft) off Mount Index Road, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail — roughly 3.6-4.1 miles (accounts vary slightly) and about 2,000 ft of gain, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur around mile 1.6 and switchbacking up to Lake Serene (~2,500 ft). At the lake, leave the maintained trail for the unofficial climbers' path that traverses talus and large boulders around the west side of the lake; in early summer this crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow/ice at the lake's edge. Continue up talus beneath the imposing north/east face of North Index toward the cirque below the Norwegian Buttresses, then work up through the brushy base of the wall — steepening mossy slabs and brush that some parties rope up for before reaching clean rock on the buttress proper. Reliable water is available at Lake Serene and its outlet creek, but not higher on the talus approach, so fill up at the lake. Plan roughly 2-3 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, more with a loaded pack for a multi-day ascent.
approach_variant_names: Lake Serene to the foot of the buttress
current.descent: Bluebell is descended by rappelling the route, not by a walk-off. Every belay is bolted and rigged for rappel, and the whole 2,000 ft can be rappelled on a single, uncut 70 m rope; an 80 m rope gives more flexibility. Dedicated rappel anchors set off the climbing line let you skip some belays and avoid the overhanging headwall pitches, which would otherwise leave you hanging in space. From the base, reverse the talus traverse around Lake Serene to the maintained trail.
current.detailed_rack: Use the full length of a 70m rope if rappelling on a single rope, which is recommended. Bring 16 draws, 2-4 of them alpine. All anchors are bolted and set up for rappel.

name: Standard Route
beta: The standard approach to Mount Johnson involves hiking to Royal Lake (7.2 miles, 2,650 ft gain), continuing into upper basin, then accessing Surprise Basin. From Surprise Basin, aim for the 6900-foot notch between Mount Johnson and Mount Clark. Mount Johnson sits on climber's left from this col. The route ascends via ramp systems, keeping to class 3 by skirting right of Gasp Pinnacle, then makes a final class 4 push to the summit block. Terrain is consistently loose and rotten, particularly in upper sections.
overview: Mount Johnson (7,680 ft) is the fourth-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains and the highest point in The Needles, a rugged subrange radiating north from Mount Deception above Royal Basin, in the remote eastern Olympics within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It sits just 1.34 miles north of Mount Deception, its parent peak and nearest higher neighbor. Compared to well-traveled Deception, Johnson sees relatively few ascents: accounts range from an exposed class 3-4 scramble to unavoidably loose class 4 terrain, and the long interior approach through Royal Basin means most parties treat it as a multi-day trip, frequently paired with neighboring Mount Clark via the Clark-Johnson col.

current.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, start on Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 through second-growth and then old-growth forest along the Dungeness River. At about 1 mile, bear right at the signed junction onto the Royal Basin Trail (the left fork continues up-valley toward Boulder Shelter/Constance Pass). The Royal Basin trail then climbs gradually for several miles alongside Royal Creek — the main water source for the approach — crossing it on log/plank bridges more than once; these crossings can run fast and cold during early-season snowmelt (June). Around mile 6 the grade steepens sharply for the push to Royal Lake (7.2 mi, roughly 2,500 ft gained from the trailhead), with the final mile gaining about 500 ft on looser, sometimes-eroded tread. From Royal Lake continue south up-valley on the scramblers'/climbers' path roughly another 0.8 mile and 600 ft to Upper Royal Basin (about 8 mi in, ~5,700 ft), a broad heather-and-tarn basin below Mount Deception's northeast face that most parties use as base camp (NPS wilderness permit and bear canister required; no fires; advance reservations cover June 15–Oct 15). From Upper Royal Basin the maintained trail ends; head cross-country west up heather benches and talus to the rim of the glacial moraine ringing Surprise Basin, the small hanging cirque between Mount Martin, Mount Johnson, and Mount Clark. Drop into Surprise Basin and cross its snowfields (crampons/axe often useful into July) toward the roughly 6,900 ft notch/col between Johnson (climber's left) and Clark (climber's right) — this is the standard gateway to Johnson's upper mountain. This off-trail stretch above Upper Royal Basin is loose talus and scree with genuine rockfall and route-finding hazard; helmets on from the moraine rim upward. Given the total distance (~19 miles / 30.9 km round trip) and elevation gain, most parties backpack in and camp at Upper Royal Basin, climbing Johnson as a long day from camp rather than attempting it car-to-car. Past the upper Royal Basin tarn, cross a small ridge west into Surprise Basin; in early September the glacier there had melted back to a deep blue lake, and from its shore the notch between Clark and Johnson is in direct view.
approach_variant_names: Royal Basin and Surprise Basin to the Clark–Johnson col
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit back to the ~6,900 ft Johnson–Clark notch, then retrace the talus-and-moraine descent down into Surprise Basin and back over its rim to Upper Royal Basin, from which the Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail leads back out to the trailhead. The class 4 terrain near the summit is the crux of the descent as well as the ascent — the rock is loose enough in spots that most reported difficulty on this peak comes from downclimbing it, so face in and test holds on anything above class 3. The summit chimney is downclimbed rather than rappelled; there are no fixed/bolted rappel stations reported on Johnson, so a party that wants a rope on the steepest step, particularly if the rock is wet, must rig it from a natural anchor (horn, chockstone, or slung block) of its own. The summit block has a solid class 4 crack for the direct finish, plus a cairned class 3 bypass that is the gentler way to come down.
current.detailed_rack: Light rack and a rope for exposed Class 3-4 steps
current.pro_needs: Minimal alpine pro; belay exposed steps as needed

name: Mount La Crosse Scramble
beta: This is a wilderness-approach peak rather than a technical climb: the crux is the multi-day hike in, not the summit itself. Reach LaCrosse Pass via trail from either the Duckabush or West Fork Dosewallips valley, then leave the trail for an unroped Class 2 ascent over talus, heather benches, and open ridge to the summit. No rope, rack, or technical protection is used on the standard line; sturdy boots, navigation tools, and self-sufficiency for a remote multi-day trip matter far more than climbing gear.
overview: Mount La Crosse is a Class 2 scramble summit on the Duckabush/Dosewallips divide in the seldom-visited southern interior of Olympic National Park, part of what is locally called the 'Dosewallips Group.' It rises above La Crosse Pass and Lake La Crosse (the peak's namesake), with White Mountain 0.95 mi SW and the Mount Anderson massif roughly 2.7 mi N. First climbed in 1928 by Richard Paulson, William Ryer, Paul Wiseman, and Frank Woodworth, it remains a multi-day objective with no day-hike trailhead access — reaching it requires backpacking in via the Duckabush River Trail or West Fork Dosewallips River Trail, then leaving maintained trail to scramble open Class 2 slopes above the pass.

current.approach: From US 101 near Brinnon, take Duckabush River Road (FR 2510) west — paved for the first 3.6 miles, then gravel for a total of about 6 miles — to the Duckabush trailhead (FR 2510-060). Follow the Duckabush River Trail up the valley about 16.7 miles to the La Crosse Pass Trail junction (~2,650 ft), then climb the La Crosse Pass Trail north, about 3 miles and 2,900 ft of steep switchbacks, to La Crosse Pass (5,566 ft). Leave the trail at the pass for the off-trail Class 2-3 scramble west along the ridge to the summit.
approach_variant_names: Duckabush River Trail to La Crosse Pass
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling. Reverse the ridge and talus scramble back down to LaCrosse Pass, picking your way carefully back through the loose Class 2–3 terrain (descending loose talus is where most of the slip-and-slide hazard on this route actually lives, more than on the ascent). From the pass, descend the LaCrosse Pass Trail to whichever trailhead your itinerary uses. If you're headed out the Duckabush side, be ready for a knee-punishing, steep, switchbacking drop of about 3,000 ft in roughly a mile back to the Duckabush River Trail junction — this section is loose underfoot and eroded in spots, and is meaningfully harder on tired legs descending than it is climbing. If you're exiting north toward the Dosewallips/West Fork Dosewallips, the grade down from the pass is gentler and more forgiving. In poor visibility, the open, sparsely-cairned country right around the pass and upper basin is the spot most likely to cause route-finding trouble on the way down — many parties mention losing the tread in lingering snowfields near the pass well into early summer. Rather than retrace the crest, a lower traverse back toward the pass is possible, but it crosses a deep washout gully on the sub-summit's face and is just as slow (July).
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard Class 2 route.
bivy: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
current.rope_note: No route-specific technical beta found despite searching. Class 2-3 rating is consistent with non-technical talus/ridge scrambling typical of this part of the Olympics — rope not standard.

name: South Slope - South Face (Standard Route)
beta: Mount Lago has no maintained summit trail and sees relatively few visitors given its remote, multi-day approach deep in the Pasayten Wilderness. Nearly all parties climb it from a backcountry camp at Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, ascending the South Slope-South Face - a straightforward but tedious scramble over notoriously loose rock - often combined with neighboring Mount Carru via the connecting saddle, or with Osceola Peak and Mount Rolo as part of a longer Pasayten peak-bagging trip or ridge traverse.
overview: The standard route climbs Mount Lago's loose south side: an unroped Class 2-3 scramble up talus, scree, and rocky ribs from a high camp at Shellrock Basin, typically descended via the adjacent Southwest Slope.

current.approach: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead (~2,500 ft, via SR-20 and Lost River Road/Forest Road 5400 west of Winthrop), follow the Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten Trail over Robinson Pass and down into the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage. Continue north down the valley past the first Eureka Creek Trail junction and, about 4.8 miles beyond the Whistler Cutoff, turn east on the Eureka Creek Trail up Berk Creek to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp and water source below Lago's west side. From Fred's Lake, follow the unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail (or cross-country) east across the upper Eureka Creek basin - the creek crossing can be difficult when swollen with snowmelt - to reach Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge. The shortest road-based approach is roughly 16 miles one-way, typically covered over 1-2 days.
approach_variant_names: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
current.descent: From the summit, descend the loose South Slope/South Face talus and scree, or drop via the Southwest Slope variant, which avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs. Many parties traverse instead to the Lago-Carru col to tag Mount Carru before returning to camp rather than descending fully and re-climbing. The rock is loose throughout, so move carefully, stay spread out, and watch for parties below.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed - the standard South Slope/South Face line is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble over talus, scree, and rocky ribs.
current.pro_needs: No protection is needed for this scramble route. Belay equipment is not required. Traction and stability are the primary concerns.
bivy: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps

name: South Ridge
beta: From High Pass, descend into the basin below the peak. Traverse west and ascend boulder fields and scree to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 feet. Locate the gully system in the rocky face with two narrow channels 30 feet apart; take the right channel and ascend the narrow then open gully to broken rock to attain the ridge top. Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the summit. Most of ridge top has a way trail and the route is partially marked with cairns after leaving the basin, but cairns may be far apart and the way trail may disappear for long stretches. If you lose cairns or way trail most gullies probably work though some may be more difficult than others.
overview: A striking reddish peak in the Border Peaks group of the Mount Baker Wilderness, 1.4 miles south of the Canada–US border and immediately southeast of taller American Border Peak. The rust color comes from oxidized iron in the peak's phyllite and greenstone rock. First climbed September 11, 1908 by James J. McArthur's party, it's now one of the most popular scrambles near Mount Baker, typically done from a Twin Lakes camp and often paired with American Border Peak.

current.approach: Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065 (the last 2 miles are rough, high-clearance terrain — many parties park lower and walk the road). From the trailhead, follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) briefly; at about 0.5 mile a signed junction splits left to Winchester Lookout and right onto the High Pass Trail (#676) — take the right fork. High Pass Trail #676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain (steep, exposed snowfields can linger here into August — an ice axe and snow-travel experience are recommended until the chute melts out), then continues up over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the old tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is reached roughly 2 miles / 1.5–2 hours from the trailhead and makes a scenic, if exposed, campsite. There is no reliable water past this point in late season, so treat/carry water from Twin Lakes or early snowmelt. Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends; an unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100–200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face (around 6,400 ft you pass a small cliff band). Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 ft. Here the route-finding crux: locate a gully system cut into the rock face — of two narrow parallel channels about 30 feet apart, take the right-hand one. Ascend the narrowing gully, which opens into broken rock, to gain the crest of the south ridge. Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit; a faint boot path and scattered cairns mark much of this stretch but both disappear for long sections, so be prepared to route-find. Total distance is roughly 8–10 miles round trip with on the order of 3,500–4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain (the up-and-over via Low Pass and High Pass adds real gain beyond straight-line distance to the summit). The rock throughout — especially the gully and upper ridge — is notoriously loose and crumbly by Cascades standards; helmets are strongly recommended and parties should keep group size small (6 or fewer) and spread out to manage rockfall risk to those below.
approach_variant_names: Twin Lakes, High Pass Trail #676 over Low Pass, then the basin to the southwest spur
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no technical descent gear needed and this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, follow the ridge crest (favoring the west side) back down to where you gained it, then descend the gully system, taking the same right-hand channel used on the way up; this loose, narrow gully is the most hazard-prone part of the descent (parties frequently trigger rockfall here even while descending carefully — down-climb one at a time or spread well apart, and keep helmets on). Below the gully, cross the broken rock and scree back down to the southwest spur (~6,900 ft) and continue down through the boulder fields and basin to regain the climbers' path near High Pass, watching for the intermittent cairns since the way trail vanishes in spots. From High Pass, retrace the High Pass Trail (#676) back over Low Pass, across the avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain (glissading or plunge-stepping lingering snow here can save time in early/mid season, but stay alert to runout hazard), and down the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) to the Twin Lakes Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No technical gear required; a few pieces optional for confidence on the steeper steps.
current.pro_needs: Minimal to none.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Mount Lawson has no summit trail. Climbers follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream through old-growth rainforest, then cut off-trail to gain the peak's slopes to the 5,401-foot summit. The scrambling itself is only Class 2 with no technical climbing, but route-finding through dense old-growth forest and brush, combined with three unbridged river fords on the approach, make this a serious, rarely-repeated wilderness undertaking rather than a casual outing.
overview: Mount Lawson (5,401 ft) is a heavily timbered, rarely climbed summit deep in the southern Olympic interior, within Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. Its 2,521 ft of prominence ranks it among the more prominent secondary peaks in the range (roughly #6 by prominence in the Olympic Mountains), but it sees little traffic — no first-ascent date or party is on record. The standard route (Route 1, Grade I, Class 3) climbs the peak's North Ridge from the North Fork Quinault River drainage.

current.approach: Via the North Fork Quinault Trailhead (North Shore Road), hike the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter until you are below Lawson's steep north flanks, which come into view approaching Twelve Mile flat — the fords at Wild Rose Creek and Elip Creek can be difficult or impassable in high water — then ford the North Fork and leave the trail, climbing off-trail directly up Lawson's north side.
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: down the North Ridge to the top of the chute, then down-climb the loose chute back to the valley floor — this is the most hazard-prone part of the descent, since the same scree and rockbands that were merely tedious going up become genuinely slippery and rockfall-prone with tired legs and no rope; move one at a time through any narrows and stay alert for parties below. At the bottom, re-ford the North Fork Quinault River (same knee-to-thigh-deep crossing as the approach — check levels, as afternoon snowmelt can raise it) to regain the maintained trail, then simply walk the North Fork Quinault River Trail back out to the trailhead, re-fording Elip and Wild Rose Creeks en route. There is no rappelling on this route: it is a scramble/walk-off (Grade I, Class 3 via the North Ridge, 'Basic Snow/Rock Scramble', or Class 2 hiking), and nothing on it involves fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work — a hand line could be a reasonable precaution for a mixed-experience party on the loose upper chute or on lingering early-season snow, but it is not a technical necessity.
bivy: Sixteen Mile Camp — the base directly under Mount Lawson
current.rope_note: A difficult scramble over rubble; Class 3 rating implies hands-on scrambling but not roped climbing. Helmet and ice axe (early season) standard.

name: Harniss Chute
beta: Documented as an alternate class 3 scrambling line to Mount Lincoln's summit, climbing a chute/gully rather than the open south ridge; reached from the same Flapjack Lakes approach as the standard route. Detailed pitch-by-pitch or turn-by-turn beta is not available.
overview: A class 3 gully variation to Mount Lincoln's standard south-ridge scramble, also approached from Flapjack Lakes.

current.approach: Same approach as the standard route: Staircase trailhead to Flapjack Lakes via the North Fork Skokomish and Flapjack Lakes Trails, then off-trail toward Mount Lincoln.
current.descent: The way off is the standard scramble, reversed back to Flapjack Lakes - the same approach this variation uses to reach the peak. No turn-by-turn description of the descent exists, so treat the line down as class 3 route-finding rather than a path to follow. In the chute itself, keep the party close together and out from under each other: confined gully terrain concentrates rockfall, and a party strung out in it is above itself.
bivy: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out

name: North Ridge from Flapjack Lakes
beta: From Flapjack Lakes, either contour around to the right or climb east and then south over the forested ridge to the head of the Madeline Creek basin. Exposed rock scrambling from there gains the north ridge, which leads south to the summit. The 5,700-ft north peak, the prominent point seen from the lakes, is not the top; keep it on your left. Allow about three hours from the lakes. The scrambling is class 3 for most of its length, with a class 4 chockstone move near the summit. The terrain is loose: steep duff and scree below the ridge, the chockstone gully and a boulder field, and an airy knife-edge near the top, so route-finding and care matter as much as difficulty. Most parties camp at the lakes; car-to-car it is a very long day. A different, easier line climbs the ridge south of the peak from lower on the valley trail, but its old trail burned in 1985 and is largely gone.
overview: Mount Lincoln (5,868 ft) is the second-highest summit on Sawtooth Ridge in the southeastern Olympic Mountains, on the shared boundary of Olympic National Park and the Mount Skokomish Wilderness (Olympic National Forest), Mason County. Its parent peak, Mount Cruiser (6,104 ft), sits 1.1 miles northeast; Lincoln has two sub-summits, North Peak (5,690 ft) and Southwest Peak (5,486 ft). Flapjack Lakes lie in a basin directly west/below the north sub-peak. The mountain is built of Eocene-age basalt from the same accretionary-wedge processes that formed the rest of the Olympics. First climbed in 1932 by Ken Soult and F.S. Harmon, Lincoln sees relatively few ascents (fewer than 30 logged) because the standard Flapjack Lakes approach involves notoriously tricky, unmarked route-finding.

current.approach: Approach via the Staircase / North Fork Skokomish trail (7.5 mi to Flapjack Lakes, ~3,100 ft gain) to Flapjack Lakes, then off-trail into the Sawtooth Ridge to the base of the climbing. Usually an overnight trip. Both the North Fork Skokomish River Trail beyond the Staircase Rapids Loop and the Flapjack Lakes Trail have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire. The Staircase road and campground reopened on July 8, 2026, but no reopening date had been announced for the trails as of September 2026, so confirm with Olympic National Park that the trail (not just the Staircase road and campground) is open before planning a trip. A largely abandoned alternate line follows an old trail up the south end of Sawtooth Ridge, starting about 2.4 miles up the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish trail; it has been in poor condition and rarely used since the 1985 Beaver Fire.
approach_variant_names: Flapjack Lakes and Sawtooth Ridge
current.descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line rather than descending a different route. Downclimb off the summit block through the gully system back to the Sawtooth Ridge crest, then drop off its west side by a steep gully (dirt first, then scree, talus and boulders) into the forest and work back through the brush to Flapjack Lakes. From there it's a long but straightforward hike down the Flapjack Lakes Trail / North Fork Skokomish River Trail to Staircase. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed rappel stations, bolted anchors, or documented rope-descent points were found for the standard scramble route, so rappels = 0. The crux is reversing the airy class 3+ (occasional class-4-feeling move) terrain right off the summit block and negotiating chockstones/ledges partway down the gully; a short handline for less-experienced party members on this section is a reasonable precaution some parties use, but it is not a technical anchor-and-rope rappel. Primary descent hazards: route-finding (several similar-looking gully systems seam the south face — parties have reported descending the wrong chute/chockstone gully and encountering sketchy downclimbing before regaining the correct line or Madeline Creek drainage), loose rock/choss on the ridge and gully walls, and lingering snow in the descent gully into midsummer (ice axe useful into July). Plan for a long day — trip reports commonly cite 11–14+ hours car-to-car — and carry a headlamp and extra water for the trail miles back to Staircase.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped climb for most parties, but some parties carry a rope with a few slings/small cams for the most exposed 3rd/4th-class moves (especially if also tagging the nearby Southwest Lincoln sub-summit).
rack: 30m rope + a few slings (optional, for the Class 4/low-5th chockstone move near the summit)
current.pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow in the approach gullies.
bivy: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
current.rope_note: Standard Scramble via Flapjack Lakes/Sawtooth Ridge (Staircase approach); Class 3 ridge terrain, second-highest point on Sawtooth Ridge. Steep snow early season needs ice axe; route not roped by standard parties.

name: Fremont Glacier
beta: Approach via Thunder Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass (19.6 mi, 4,900 ft gain from trailhead), then traverse northward 2 miles across heather and alpine meadows to Fremont Glacier at 8,000 feet. Ascend the gentle glacier to the south ridge (Hogsback), negotiate a snow-filled gully through cliff bands, and scramble Class 3-4 rock via ledges on the east side of the summit ridge to the summit.
overview: A massive multi-summited peak above Thunder Creek and Park Creek Pass, Mount Logan is one of the high Bulger summits of the North Cascades. The Fremont Glacier route is the standard line, climbing the glacier on the southwest side to a final scramble onto the true summit.

current.approach: Start at Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR 20 mile 130 (elevation 1,060 ft). Follow Thunder Creek Trail south for approximately 16-18 miles to Thunder Basin camp around 6,000 ft. From Thunder Basin, cross meadows and begin ascending. Traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, gaining approximately 2 miles to reach Fremont Glacier at 8,000 feet. Campsites exist at Thunder Basin and other designated locations along the approach.
approach_variant_names: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, most parties can downclimb the exposed Class 3-4 summit tower and the U-notch below it with care (a belayed downclimb works for many groups), but this step is steep and exposed enough that some parties choose to rappel roughly 30-50 ft off the summit block down to the snow hogback at the glacier's upper edge rather than downclimb it with packs on. There are no fixed/bolted anchors reported on this seldom-traveled route — any rappel is built from natural gear (a rock horn or chockstone with a sling, or a picket if snow conditions allow), so carry a small rack of slings and be prepared to leave gear behind. After regaining the hogback, rope up again to reverse the Fremont Glacier crossing, drop back to high camp, then retrace the cross-country descent through Thunder Basin to rejoin the Thunder Creek Trail for the long, mostly flat hike out. The Thunder/Park Creek footlog crossings can be genuinely nerve-wracking if you're crossing them in the dark on a long summit-day exit, and the Thunder Creek ford is worth respecting if water is up.
current.detailed_rack: A short rock rack for the summit scramble plus full glacier rescue equipment.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock pro on the finish; glacier protection as conditions dictate.
bivy: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
Valley camps on the walk in

name: Banded Glacier
beta: Approach via Easy Pass (6,500 ft) from Highway 20 mile 151, descend into Fisher Basin, then off-trail climb to Banded Glacier basin. Ascend unstable scree slopes to reach the glacier, cross the Banded Glacier to meet the NE ridge at approximately 8,800 feet, then scramble Class 3-4 rock to the summit. The critical transition point is gaining the NE ridge on solid rock rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. (A longer, always-open alternate approach exists via the Thunder Creek/Fisher Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground — ~13 mi one-way vs. ~10 mi via Easy Pass — useful when Easy Pass Trailhead is gated by SR 20's seasonal closure.)
overview: Mount Logan is a remote North Cascades summit. The Banded Glacier route is the standard line, ascending the glacier on the north side to a Class 3-4 scramble to the summit.

current.approach: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, descend into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier, about 10 miles one way. When SR 20 is closed at Easy Pass, the longer Thunder Creek way in (about 13 miles) starts at Colonial Creek Campground. In late June the Easy Pass trail can vanish under snow near the top; keep traversing west at pass level before picking up the switchbacks down to Fisher Creek.
approach_variant_names: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
Thunder Creek and Fisher Creek
current.descent: Reverse the route: descend the Banded Glacier, climb back over the col toward Fisher Creek, and hike back out over Easy Pass to the trailhead (or exit via the longer Thunder Creek Trail alternate if Easy Pass Trailhead is inaccessible).
current.detailed_rack: Glacier travel kit; light rack for summit rocks
current.pro_needs: Crevasse rescue gear; minimal rock pro near the top
bivy: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier

name: Douglas Glacier
beta: Approach via Easy Pass (6,500 ft) from Highway 20 mile 151, descend into Fisher Creek valley, cross Fisher Creek, travel up Douglas Creek valley (extremely brushy, slow progress), gain Douglas Glacier basin, ascend steep glacier with steeper ice/snow sections to col, traverse to meet Banded Glacier, then scramble Class 3-4 rock to summit via standard summit block.
overview: The Douglas Glacier route climbs Mount Logan from the southeast and is rated Grade III, Class 4. It's a well-regarded, reasonably-paced 3-day objective for a fit team, approached via the Easy Pass Trail and a cross-country descent into Fisher Basin.

current.approach: Start at Easy Pass Trailhead at Highway 20 mile 151 (elevation 3,700 ft). Hike 3.5 miles gaining 2,800 feet to Easy Pass (6,500 ft). Descend into Fisher Basin via steep scenic trail through alpine meadows and forest (1.5 miles). Continue to Fisher Creek valley floor and established campsites. From camp area, cross Fisher Creek via large fallen log and travel east side of Douglas Creek valley on faint climber's path. This transition from forest to open terrain is where the route becomes extremely challenging—travelers encounter a vast field of slide alder and other brush, 10+ feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, with small rocky stream channels crisscrossing the ground. Progress is measured in inches per minute. Off-trail navigational skill critical. In late June the Easy Pass trail is mostly clear for the first mile or two, then lost under snow; past the pass the trail continues west at pass level.
approach_variant_names: Easy Pass, the Douglas Creek alder, then the west-side gully to the polished slabs
current.descent: Descend the Banded Glacier via the Banded-Douglas col to reach the Fisher Creek basin, or reverse the Douglas Glacier with care back toward Easy Pass. A short rappel from the false summit drops to the saddle before the final class 4 summit block.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier travel and crevasse rescue kit plus a few screws/pickets for steeper sections
current.pro_needs: Screws/pickets for the steeper ice; crevasse rescue gear

name: Southwest Ridge Route
beta: An off-trail scramble approached via the Swamp Creek drainage off the Agnes Creek/PCT corridor. From a Swamp Creek camp, travelers cross Swamp Creek, climb through brush and open basin to about 4,000', then work up scree and talus (with lingering snow possible) toward a roughly 7,300' notch on the southwest ridge. From the notch, a traverse below a prominent white vertical rock band on grassy ledges leads to an exposed, narrowing class 3 gully; the final ~200' to the summit climbs through loose, stacked boulders (choss).
overview: Mount Lyall is a remote, seldom-climbed summit above the Agnes Creek and Swamp Creek drainages south of Stehekin, sitting near the boundary of the Stephen Mather Wilderness (North Cascades National Park) and the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It is reached by a long trail approach from the head of Lake Chelan; the peak itself is a short but genuinely exposed scramble, not a simple talus walk.

current.approach: Via passenger ferry or floatplane from Chelan to Stehekin, then the PCT/Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge; follow the Agnes Creek Trail and Swamp Creek drainage to Lyall's west basin. Swamp Creek Camp is about 8 miles from High Bridge, and most parties camp there. From the west basin, climb talus and heather to gain the southwest ridge, passing below a distinctive band of white rock; the route narrows into an exposed Class 3 gully near the summit, finishing over stacked Class 3-4 boulders to the summit block.
approach_variant_names: Agnes Creek and the Swamp Creek drainage to the west basin
current.descent: Downclimb the Class 3-4 boulders and exposed gully back into the west basin, then reverse the southwest ridge and basin descent to Swamp Creek and the Agnes Creek Trail.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection or roped climbing is documented on this route; it is typically done as an unroped scramble.
bivy: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found (searches returned unrelated Mount Lyell/Lyall peaks in CA/Alberta). Class 3-4 rating suggests exposed scrambling where some parties may choose a short handline for the class 4 crux, though not standard for all parties.

name: South Route
beta: Most parties start from the Merritt Lake Trailhead, hike the maintained trail to Merritt Lake, then follow the Nason Ridge Trail for about a mile and turn uphill on an unsigned boot path that climbs steep forest to Mastiff's southeast ridge (other lines reach the peak from the Crescent Lake basin via the Howard-Mastiff ridge, or up the northeast ridge from Lost Lake). On the ridge, follow the crest -- staying just below it to avoid small cliffs and dense subalpine trees -- to the summit. The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake, so navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge. Many parties combine the peak with Mount Howard (1 mile west) as a single long day.
overview: Mount Mastiff (6,747 ft) is the third-highest point on Nason Ridge, roughly a mile east of Mount Howard (7,063 ft), overlooking Lake Wenatchee and the US-2 corridor between Leavenworth and Stevens Pass. The South (Southeast Ridge) Route climbs from the Merritt Lake trailhead through old-growth forest to Merritt Lake, then leaves the maintained trail to follow the ridge crest to the broad, flat summit — a Class 2 scramble with one or two Class 3 moves around rock gendarmes, popular as a long day trip and often paired with Mount Howard.

current.approach: From US-2 near milepost 76 (about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass / 24 miles west of Leavenworth), turn onto Forest Road 657 (rough, high-clearance recommended) and drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,050 ft). Hike the Merritt Lake Trail up toward the ridge, connecting with the Nason Ridge Trail; figure a long day (roughly 10 miles round trip, ~4,900 ft gain for Mastiff alone) or an overnight via Merritt or Lost Lake.
approach_variant_names: Merritt Lake Trail and Nason Ridge Trail
current.descent: Descend by the same southeast-ridge line, staying close to the ridge crest and again favoring the east side to reverse the gendarme bypass near 6,125 ft (loose rock and talus underfoot - go slow, this is the section most prone to kicking rocks onto anyone below). Where the boot path leaves the crest, follow it down through the forest to the Nason Ridge Trail, walk back about a mile to the Merritt Lake junction, and take the maintained Merritt Lake Trail down to the trailhead. This is entirely a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved anywhere on this route; the terrain throughout is Class 2-3 scrambling on talus, scree, and broken rock. The only real descent hazards are loose rock (helmet recommended, especially in groups), the boot path off the ridge fading into open heather and talus with no maintained tread - fog or flat late-day light makes it genuinely hard to relocate - and the fact that the route should not be down-climbed wet or icy since the rock gets slick.
current.pro_needs: None -- this is a non-technical talus/scree/ridge scramble with no fixed protection or belaying involved on the standard line.
bivy: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble with talus, bushwhacking, and gendarmes on the ridge. Trip reports cite helmets and ice axes; rope not part of standard gear list.

name: West Face
beta: Two variations reach the same Class 4 summit ridge: (1) climb the steep snow finger between Mount Mathias and Glacier Pass, then scramble Class 4 rock on the ridge to the summit; or (2) climb steep gullies to the Mercury-Mathias col and take the Class 4 ridge from there. Both require prior glacier travel across the Blue Glacier/Hoh Glacier system and are often combined with Mount Mercury or a Mount Olympus trip, since the approach alone is a multi-day undertaking.
overview: Mount Mathias (7,156 ft) is a high summit of the Mount Olympus massif in the interior of Olympic National Park, flanked by the Blue Glacier to the west and the Hoh Glacier to the east. It is reached by long wilderness approaches, culminating in a short but genuine Class 4 scramble on the summit ridge above Glacier Pass or the Mercury-Mathias col.

current.approach: Drive the paved Upper Hoh Road to its end at the Hoh Ranger Station (578 ft). Hike the Hoh River Trail 17.2 miles to Glacier Meadows (~4,200-4,300 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the range (note: a washed-out section partway up requires a fixed ladder/rope crossing). From Glacier Meadows, follow the way trail 0.8 mi to the top of the Blue Glacier lateral moraine, continue along the moraine crest ~0.2 mi, then descend onto the Blue Glacier and ascend snow slopes around rock islands to the crest of Snow Dome (6,600 ft). From Snow Dome, rope up and continue up the upper Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass (the saddle between Mathias and the East Peak of Olympus, at the head of the Hoh Glacier), then gain the base of either the Mathias snow finger or the steep gullies leading to the Mercury-Mathias col.
approach_variant_names: Hoh River and the Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass
current.descent: Descend by the same line used on ascent: downclimb the Class 4 summit ridge back to the top of the snow finger, then plunge-step or downclimb the 35–40° snow finger back to Glacier Pass. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed rappel stations are reported on Mathias itself, and no rappels are specifically documented for this line; treat the snow finger and the loose upper ridge as the descent crux (rockfall and a fall-arrest-consequence slope, not technical lowering). If the snow has gone to hard ice/firm neve late in the season, some parties choose to belay or downclimb facing in rather than plunge-stepping. From Glacier Pass, reverse the approach: cross back onto the Blue Glacier and descend it — passing the Snow Dome bootpack and exiting via the glacier's lateral/terminal moraine — down to Glacier Meadows Camp, and out the Hoh River Trail to the trailhead (roughly 2 days of hiking/glacier travel from Glacier Pass back to the car). Watch for rockfall on the loose upper mountain as the day warms, softening snow bridges on the Hoh/Blue Glacier crossings later in the day, and the washed-out section of the Hoh River Trail, crossed on a fixed ladder, on the way out.
current.detailed_rack: Standard glacier-travel kit for the Blue Glacier/Hoh Glacier crossing: rope-team gear and cordage. No technical rock rack is typically carried — the Class 4 ridge above the col/snow finger is generally scrambled unroped by parties comfortable with the exposure and loose rock.
current.pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used; the summit ridge is Class 4 scrambling, generally climbed unroped. The mandatory gear is for the approach: rope, harness, and crevasse-rescue kit for the Blue Glacier and Hoh Glacier crossings.
current.rope_note: The Blue Glacier on the approach is crevassed and requires a rope; the Class 4 ridge scrambling on broken sedimentary rock itself is typically unroped by experienced parties, but a short rope aids confidence on exposed sections.

name: Entiat Ice Fall
beta: From a bivy above Ice Lakes, over the ridge from Leroy Creek Basin, descend to the Entiat Glacier surface, cross the ablation zone, and climb the icefall's short vertical ice steps and ramps between crevasses (running belay) before turning right onto ~900 vertical feet of crumbly 4th/low-5th class rock leading to the summit. The glacier has receded substantially since Fred Beckey's era, when the route reportedly had 9 pitches of ice; today's icefall is shorter and more variable year to year.
overview: A true alpine route climbing what remains of the receding Entiat Icefall on the north side of the peak, then finishing up ~900 ft of loose 4th and low-5th class rock to the summit.

current.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the North Face: Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft) via FR 6211, up the Phelps Creek Trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the climber's trail into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,100-6,200 ft, ~5 miles). From camp, continue toward the Seven Fingered Jack-Maude col/Ice Lakes area and descend to the Entiat Glacier to reach the icefall.
approach_variant_names: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to a bivy at Ice Lakes, then the notch onto the Entiat Glacier
current.descent: From the summit, descend via the South Ridge, which in good conditions takes only about 30 minutes from the summit back to the ridge/basin area, considerably faster than the ascent.
current.detailed_rack: Ice screws and pickets for the icefall's short vertical steps and ramps between crevasses, plus a light rock rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the ~900 ft of 4th/low-5th class rock above - though protection on the rock is scarce due to crumbly rock quality, and many parties rely on running belays rather than placed gear.
current.pro_needs: Bring both ice and rock protection; the upper rock is poor quality so don't expect reliable placements - running belays are common practice here.
bivy: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds

name: North Slopes from Lake Valhalla
beta: Mount McCausland's only established access is this north-side approach: Smithbrook Trail #1590 climbs to Union Gap on the PCT, then the route follows the PCT south before cutting off onto an unsigned but well-trodden boot path that switchbacks north up open heather meadows to the 5,747 ft summit. The whole outing is about 6.4 miles round trip with roughly 1,800 ft of elevation gain and is popular as a moderate day hike/scramble; there is no documented technical first ascent or climbing route on the peak.
overview: Mount McCausland rises just above scenic Lake Valhalla near Stevens Pass and is among the most accessible scrambles in the corridor. An unmarked climber's path leaves the PCT at a saddle just before the trail drops to the lake, climbing steeply through heather, brush, and loose rock to the broad summit.

current.approach: From US Highway 2 about 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, turn onto Smith Brook Road (Forest Road 6700) and follow the gravel road roughly 2.6-2.8 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead (el. ~4,000 ft; no fee, no Northwest Forest Pass required); the road is closed to vehicles under a storm-damage order effective May 20, 2026 through December 31, 2027 unless lifted sooner, so confirm it has reopened before driving. Hike Smithbrook Trail #1590 through old-growth forest, entering the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness at about 0.5 mile, and continue to Union Gap (el. ~4,600-4,688 ft) at roughly 1.0-1.3 miles, where the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn south (left) on the PCT for about 1.4 miles through forest with views toward Lichtenberg Mountain and Nason Ridge, to an unnamed gap at about 5,100 ft. Just before/at this gap, an unmarked but obvious boot path breaks off to the north through heather meadows, climbing a steep, sometimes brushy and eroded 0.5 mile (about 650 ft of additional gain) to the true summit.
approach_variant_names: Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap and the Lake Valhalla crest trail
current.descent: Reverse the boot path down to the PCT junction, then descend the Smithbrook Trail to the trailhead. Lake Valhalla is an easy side trip by continuing straight on the PCT from the junction instead of turning off.
current.rope_note: Short, low-elevation (~1,800ft gain) Class 2 scramble near Lake Valhalla; some rock scrambling near the summit but rated only 'mildly technical.' No technical rock or snow gear needed beyond trekking poles/traction in shoulder season.

name: Standard Route
beta: The standard route is less about technical difficulty and more about remoteness: a multi-day wilderness approach up the North Fork Quinault River and through Seattle Basin precedes a day of ridge scrambling, a sidehill traverse beneath Mt. Noyes, a loose couloir/snow col, and a short but real 5th-class crux on crumbly sandstone just below the summit. The easiest route is rated Class 3, but multiple parties in the 2020s describe an exposed ~25 ft 5.2 lead pitch protected with a small rack and rope, descended via two rappels — treat this as harder than a pure scramble.
overview: Mount Meany (6,695 ft) is a remote summit in the Quinault Group of Olympic National Park's Bailey Range area, with small permanent snowfields on its north and east slopes. There is no maintained trail to the top; the standard scramble route climbs the east side via the Noyes-Meany col, reached only after a multi-day wilderness approach. First climbed August 8, 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Lorenz Nelson, and Peter McGregor.

current.approach: No maintained trail reaches the peak. Most parties approach via the Elwha River Trail from Whiskey Bend and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass into the Bailey Range highline route, or via the North Fork Quinault River Trail from the North Fork Quinault trailhead (not Graves Creek, which serves the East Fork and Enchanted Valley) to Low Divide, then up through Seattle Basin to the saddle just east of Mount Noyes. Either approach involves 3-5+ days of off-trail travel, river fords, and remote high camps before reaching the Noyes-Meany col. From late August into September, parties leave the Skyline Trail near 4,800 ft, cross a flat dry-tarn plateau around 4,900 ft, then sidehill to the Noyes-Seattle col; in cloud it is easy to aim for the wrong col.
approach_variant_names: Seattle Basin to the Noyes–Meany saddle
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than a separate walk-off. From the true summit, downclimb the short exposed crest/corkscrew section back to the top of the summit block's crux pitch. Two independent parties describe needing two rappels here to get down the steep upper step of the southeast ridge/northeast face terrain (the same short low-5th-class face and exposed crest climbed on the way up) before a final downclimb/traverse regains the sloping ledge and the Meany-Noyes col. Anchors reported here are natural/improvised - slung horns, blocks, or a hand-placed piton in a crack - not bolted or fixed hardware, so carry a small rack (stoppers, a few pitons or a hammer if you want backup, and slings) for building gauge anchors; do not expect anything pre-equipped. Given the short pitch heights described (a roughly 25-foot crux face and a similarly short second step), a single 30-40m rope rappelled should cover each stretch, though most parties simply carry their climbing rope (commonly a 30-60m single) and rappel it as a single strand or doubled depending on length and anchor position - exact rope length isn't specified, so size it to your rack and be ready to build an intermediate anchor if a single rappel doesn't reach. Below the rappels, reverse the loose rock couloir and the scree/dirt sidehill beneath Mt. Noyes back to the Noyes-Meany saddle, then cross-country back down to Seattle Basin camp. From there, reverse the full approach: Skyline route down to Low Divide, the North Fork Quinault ford, and the North Fork Quinault River Trail back to the trailhead. Loose rock on the couloir and sidehill, and the exposed, unprotected downclimbing between the rappels, are the primary descent hazards - this is not a beginner scramble descent despite the 'scrambling' classification.
current.detailed_rack: A rope (30 m or longer) and a small rack of stoppers, a few pitons and slings: the roughly 25 ft 5.2 pitch below the summit is led, and both rappels come off anchors you build yourself.
current.pro_needs: Small rack of stoppers, a few pitons and slings for the 5.2 pitch and the rappel anchors
bivy: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones

name: Standard Scramble (Deception Creek / Royal Basin)
beta: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, hike the Royal Basin trail to Royal Lake/Upper Royal Basin, then climb a steep snowfield to the ridge notch (locally called Royal Pass or Deception Pass) dividing Royal and Deception basins. Descend into Deception Basin, cross the stagnant, minimally-crevassed Mystery Glacier to a col (~6,700 ft) on the peak's east side, then work up mixed scree, snow, and rock on the south side of the mountain, finishing with a short, exposed Class 4 breccia section/gully to the summit block.
overview: Mount Mystery (7,639 ft) is a remote, glaciated summit in the eastern Olympic Mountains at the head of Deception Creek, just south of Mount Deception. Named circa 1915 by USFS official G.A. Whitehead for its regal appearance in fog, it's a big, classic-looking peak that's rarely climbed because of the long approach and notoriously rotten rock. A small remnant glacier (Mystery Glacier) sits on its east side; the summit is walled in by Deception and Constance, with Mount Olympus visible in the distance.

current.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (Forest Road 2870, Olympic National Forest), follow the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2) about 1 mile, then Royal Creek Trail (#832) into Buckhorn Wilderness and across the park boundary to Royal Lake / Royal Basin (roughly 6-7 miles and ~2,500 ft of gain from the trailhead). From upper Royal Basin, continue off-trail cross-country over Royal Pass (~6,500 ft) into Deception Basin, then up basins/gullies (via the Mystery Glacier or the south ridge) to the base of the summit block. Expect a multi-day backcountry trip for most parties.
approach_variant_names: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin, over the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
Home Lake and Constance Pass, reaching Deception Basin from the south
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line. The technical crux is downclimbing back from the summit block to the south ridge notch through the same loose, exposed class 3–4 gully; some parties make two single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the saddle/notch rather than downclimbing the whole thing, then downclimbing the remaining class 2–3 terrain. A single 60m rope is sufficient for each of the two rappels; no bolted or fixed hardware is reported anywhere on this remote, seldom-traveled Olympic National Park peak, so anchors should be assumed natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) — build and back these up carefully given the rotten rock. Below the notch, downclimb/scramble the mixed rock-and-snow traverse back to the top of Mystery Glacier, then descend the low-angle glacier (parties commonly glissade or down-scramble it quickly in good conditions) back to the Deception Basin camp/gravel bars. From Deception Basin, re-climb the loose scree traverse to the Royal/Deception divide and descend the 35–40° snow slope back into Upper Royal Basin — many glissade this if runout is clean, but check for exposed rock in late season since a fall here would run a long way. From Upper Royal Basin, follow the maintained Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail back down past Royal Lake to the trailhead. Note: a different, longer traverse exit continues past the south ridge notch over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips/Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels required — that is a valid but distinct high-route variant, not the standard reverse-the-ascent descent described above.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties; some parties carry a 30m rope and a few pickets/small rack (e.g., a couple of nuts) for the steep snow descent and as a bail option at the notch below the summit.
rack: A couple of nuts and pickets (optional bail/protection option at the notch)
current.pro_needs: No technical rock pro required on the standard line; a short rope and a light alpine rack are sometimes carried for the exposed Class 3 summit moves and for belaying less-experienced partners.
current.rope_note: Standard Scramble via Royal Basin includes a mellow glacier approach and one pitch of 4th-class scrambling near the summit; most parties carry a short rope for this pitch plus glacier-travel gear for the approach.

name: Mount Norton Scramble
beta: Mount Norton has no maintained summit trail. The accepted easiest route follows the Elwha River Trail south from Whiskey Bend to the Hayes River area, then leaves the trail for cross-country Class 2 travel (talus, heather, open forest) up the mountain's flank to the summit. No technical climbing gear is required, but off-trail route-finding, brush, and the remoteness of the approach are the main obstacles.
overview: Mount Norton is a 6,319 ft summit deep in Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, rising above the confluence of the Elwha and Hayes Rivers in the park's remote interior. It has no maintained summit trail. Originally named "Mount Egan" in 1890 by the Seattle Press Expedition, it was renamed in 1925 by USFS official G.A. Whitehead for his friend Ernest Norton; Pat Cummins made the first recorded ascent in 1947. The peak is defined by extreme local relief — its east face climbs 3,200 ft above Hayes River in under a mile, and its west slopes drop 4,400 ft to the Elwha valley over about two miles. The standard route is Class 2, but published trip-report beta is sparse; this is a serious, multi-day wilderness objective rather than a roadside or day scramble.

current.approach: From the Madison Falls trailhead (the end of vehicle access since November 2017 flood damage), walk or bike roughly 7 miles up the closed road to the Whiskey Bend trailhead, then follow the Elwha River Trail about 16 miles into the park interior to the Hayes River Guard Station before leaving the trail to scramble Mount Norton.
current.descent: This is a non-technical Class 2 scramble route with no rappels documented or reasonably expected — descend by reversing the same east-slope line back down to the Hayes River drainage, then walk out the Elwha River Trail to Whiskey Bend (plus the extra road miles back to Madison Falls if that closure is still in effect). The upper scree/heather and looser rock band just below the summit ridge deserve care on the way down — this ground is more prone to slips descending than climbing, and losing the correct gully/rib on the way back into the trees can cliff you out in brush, so keep close track of your ascent line (GPS track recommended) rather than freelancing a new descent line. No rope, rack, or fixed anchors are needed under normal summer conditions.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is required on this Class 2 scramble.
bivy: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found. Olympic rock here (shale/sandstone/pillow lava) is characteristically loose — helmet essential — but Class 2-3 rating indicates non-technical scrambling without rope.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Mount Noyes is rarely climbed as a standalone objective; most parties tag it while on a multi-day scramble traverse linking Mount Christie, Noyes, Meany, and Seattle from a base camp near Low Divide or Seattle Creek/Twelvemile Shelter. The standard line follows steep talus, heather, and (early season) snow to one of the peak's bounding cols, then scrambles class 2-3 terrain along the summit ridge to the top. Parties describe the approach itself -- a long sidehill traverse across eroded, loose gullies beneath the peak's east and west aspects -- as the real crux of the day, more consequential than the summit scrambling.
overview: Mount Noyes is a peak in the cluster of summits around the head of the Elwha near Mount Seattle and Mount Queets, sitting at a triple divide that feeds the Elwha, Queets, and Quinault watersheds. The standard route is a Class 2-3 scramble over heather, talus, and rock, reached from a high camp near Low Divide via either the long Elwha River approach or the shorter North Fork Quinault approach.

current.approach: The standard approach is the North Fork Quinault River Trail, about 16 miles one-way to a high camp at Low Divide. The Elwha River Trail from Whiskey Bend also reaches Low Divide, but it is far longer (~28 miles one-way, plus roughly 7 miles each way of hiking or biking, since the Elwha access road has been closed to vehicles beyond Madison Falls since November 2017 flood damage) and suits parties traversing from the north. From high camp, travel off-trail over talus and heather toward the Noyes-Meany col and up the standard slopes.
approach_variant_names: Low Divide and Seattle Basin to the Noyes–Meany col
Elwha River to Low Divide
current.descent: Descend the standard slopes, retracing the route back to high camp near Low Divide, then out via whichever trailhead (Whiskey Bend or North Fork Quinault) was used on approach.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard Class 2+ scramble to Noyes' summit — it is unroped talus/scree travel.
current.pro_needs: None for the summit scramble itself. Parties continuing the connecting ridge toward Mount Meany should carry a rope (a 30m rope was used in one documented account) and minimal protection for the roped downclimb/rappel on that harder link, which is a separate undertaking from the standard Noyes route.
bivy: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found; Class 2-3 rating is consistent with non-technical Olympic talus/ridge scrambling — rope not standard.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Mount Olson sees very few ascents.
