Most parties reach it as a side trip from the long Six Ridge traverse between the South Fork and North Fork Skokomish valleys: hike the South Fork Skokomish River Trail to Sundown Pass/Sundown Lake, join the Six Ridge Trail, then leave it on the primitive, unsigned way trail toward Mount Olson before finishing cross-country to the summit. There is no recorded roped climbing route, rack, or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak anywhere; it is treated purely as a bushwhack/scramble objective by Olympic peak-baggers.
overview: Mount Olson is a peak in the southeastern Olympic interior above the South Fork Skokomish valley (Mason County), within Olympic National Park. The standard route follows the primitive Six Ridge Trail to a brushy, largely unmaintained boot path along the ridge crest (known as the "Mount Olson Way") through forest, heather, and talus to a steep, loose, and slow summit scramble.

current.approach: Multi-day approach: hike the Skokomish Lower/Upper South Fork Trail (Olympic National Forest Trail #873) to the Six Ridge Trail and Sundown Pass/Lake, then follow the primitive "Mount Olson Way" boot path along Six Ridge off-trail to Olson's upper slopes. Expect significant brush and blowdowns low, easier scrambling higher up.
approach_variant_names: South Fork Skokomish Trail #873 to Sundown Pass, then the Six Ridge crest and the Mount Olson Way
current.descent: From the pass immediately east of the summit, the final climb to Mount Olson's 5,289 ft high point is a steep, unmarked scramble up a grassy/heather slope pitched around 55-60 degrees in places — hands-on, solid Class 3 — that eases and curves around the north side of the peak on a heather bench before an easy stroll to the true summit. There is no fixed hardware, cairned rappel station, or reported roped descent anywhere on this peak: parties down-climb the exact line they climbed. Descend the steep meadow/heather pitch back to the east pass, drop back into Success Basin, pass the tarn again, and reverse the loose notch/talus crossing back up and over to Camp Belview — treat the notch and the upper summit meadow as the descent crux, since both are loose, exposed, and best handled with an ice axe or trekking pole for self-arrest, especially if wet or carrying late-season snow. From Camp Belview, retrace the Six Ridge Trail through its repeated ridge crossings to Six Ridge Pass, down to Sundown Lake, back over Sundown Pass, and down the South Fork Skokomish River Trail to the trailhead — essentially the same multi-day return as the approach, in reverse. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling: rappels = 0.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection or rack is documented for this route; it is an unroped scramble/bushwhack, not a technical rock climb.
bivy: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found; Class 2-3 rating is consistent with non-technical Olympic scrambling — rope not standard.

name: Blue Glacier (Standard Route)
beta: From Glacier Meadows, descend to and cross the Blue Glacier for approximately 1 mile with crevasse avoidance. Ascend the broad Snow Dome (6,600 feet) with careful snow bridge assessment. Navigate toward Crystal Pass at 7,250 feet, then traverse to the summit block base and complete the final Class 5.3-5.4 climbing to the true summit.
overview: The standard route on Mount Olympus and the classic way to the highest, most prominent summit in the Olympic Mountains. A long rainforest approach up the Hoh River leads to the Blue Glacier; moderate glacier travel over Snow Dome and Crystal Pass gains the summit pyramid, capped by a short technical rock pitch (about 5.4) to the true West Peak.

current.approach: Start at the Hoh Ranger Station/Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (578 ft) inside Olympic National Park and follow the Hoh River Trail east. The first 10.5 miles, past the Olympus Guard Station (~9.5 mi) to Lewis Meadows (1,005 ft), are gentle, shaded old-growth rainforest walking along the braided, glacially-fed Hoh River, with numerous log/stream crossings and abundant water the whole way. Continue and cross the High Hoh Bridge (a dramatic span hundreds of feet above the gorge, ~13.2 mi) into steeper, more exposed terrain. Reach Elk Lake (2,500 ft) around mile 15, where the trail begins climbing in earnest toward Glacier Meadows (4,200-4,300 ft, ~17.2-17.5 mi), the standard base camp. In early season expect several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows requiring an ice axe and crampons. About 0.25 mile before Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout/slide area via a roughly 100 ft ladder (sometimes called the Jemrod Gully ladder) supplemented by a fixed rope; this is the crux of the hike-in for many parties. From Glacier Meadows, follow the climbers' way trail about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine (a narrow, exposed 'catwalk' with loose rock underfoot), then along the moraine crest roughly 0.2 mile before descending onto the toe of the Blue Glacier itself (watch for rockfall on this descent). No camping is permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier. From Glacier Meadows the summit is roughly 4-6 more miles and about 3,700 ft of gain, roped up for crevasse travel from the glacier's edge, by way of Snow Dome (~6,600 ft) and the upper mountain; a notable hazard en route is a large crevasse near Crystal Pass that is often 'impassable' except via a snow bridge that must be scouted each season. Late June to mid-August is the best window for a straightforward glacier crossing.
approach_variant_names: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
current.descent: Descend the same North Ridge/Blue Glacier line in reverse. From the base of the ~80 ft summit rock, the roughly Class 4 with one Class 5 (5.4-ish) step is reversed by rappel rather than downclimbed by most parties: build/clip the fixed summit anchor (recent parties note slung horns/blocks and a semi-permanent thin rappel line has appeared in some seasons, though this should not be trusted blindly) and rappel the north side of the summit block. A single-strand rappel with a 40-50m rope reaches the notch/belay ledge for most of the season; a 60m rope (doubled, ~30m per strand) is the safer bet as summer progresses and snow recedes below the block, and some parties join two ropes to make one long rappel to the base of the block instead of two shorter ones. An alternative is a single-rope rappel off the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then downclimbing the original route. Anchor material is a mix of fixed slings on horns/chockstones and natural gear (small cams in the 0.3-0.4 range have been used to back up or build anchors) rather than bolts — inspect any in-place tat before trusting it. Below the summit block, reverse the snow slope (mind the runout) back to the Snow Dome plateau, re-rope for the Blue Glacier crossing, regain the lateral moraine catwalk, and retrace the Hoh River Trail 17+ miles back to the trailhead, watching for the ladder/washout section and any lingering steep snow between Glacier Meadows and Elk Lake.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack suffices for the single ~100 ft summit pitch: alpine draws, cams in BD C4 #0.5, #0.75, #1, #2, and a set of nuts. A 60 m rope is needed to rappel the summit block.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock pro on a short pitch plus full glacier-travel and crevasse-rescue equipment for the Blue Glacier.

name: Standard Scramble (Jefferson Creek / Hamma Hamma approach)
beta: From the Jefferson Creek trailhead pullout (~2,440 ft) a faint, flagged climber's path follows the north side of Jefferson Creek through forest, boulders and windfall, steepening and thickening into brush before angling up into a rocky gully. The gully (talus, sometimes snow-filled) is followed to a small basin around 4,300 ft; from there the route continues straight up, then left up a second gully to the basin east of the true (south) summit at around 5,400 ft. From there, either the center gully or a left-hand gully — the left option featuring 45-50° snow followed by a short, loose/brushy class 4 rock step — gains the south ridge. The ridge crest is class 2, occasionally class 3, with one distinctly exposed knife-edge section requiring a class 3/4 move near the 6,154 ft summit. Most parties treat the whole thing as a long, committing scramble rather than a roped climb, though a rope is commonly carried for the class 4 step and the ridge crux.
overview: Mount Pershing (6,158 ft on LIDAR-based data, ~6,154 ft per older USGS figures; roughly 1,100+ ft of prominence) is a rugged, three-summited massif in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness of Olympic National Forest, rising above the Hamma Hamma River drainage in the southeastern Olympics near Mount Washington and Mount Ellinor. It is a demanding scramble for its modest elevation: a brushy, mostly off-trail approach from the Jefferson Creek trailhead climbs into basins below the peak, then up a steep snow-and-rock gully with a short, loose Class 4 step to the summit ridge.

current.approach: From Hoodsport, drive about 14 miles north on US 101 to Hamma Hamma River Road (FR 25); follow it roughly 6.5 miles to FR 2480, then FR 2480 about 3 miles to FR 2401, then FR 2401 roughly 7–7.5 miles to the Jefferson Creek crossing / Jefferson Lake Trailhead area (~2,440 ft). A faint boot path on the north side of the creek leads through forest and brush into the basins below Pershing's east side, then up gullies to the summit ridge. Confirm current road status with Olympic National Forest before driving — FR 2480/2401 have a history of washouts and occasional fire closures. From the boot path, the route rises via a rocky gully to a small basin around 4,300 ft, then continues into a basin east of the summit near 5,400 ft before the final snow/rock gully to the ridge.
approach_variant_names: Jefferson Creek boot path from the forest road
current.descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the ridge crest and the short Class 4 step, then descend the snow/rock gully and basins back to the Jefferson Creek trail and trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed technical rack is required — this is a scramble, not a roped rock route. Most parties carry no rock protection. Groups wanting extra security for the short loose class 4 rock step or the exposed summit knife-edge sometimes bring a 30-40m rope with a handful of slings/runners to rig a hip-belay or a quick sling-rappel off a horn, block, or tree; a light rack of nuts/small cams is optional insurance, not standard practice.
rack: 1-2 runners (optional handline on the exposed ridge section)
current.pro_needs: No fixed technical rock protection on the standard line, but the short Class 4 step and 45–50° snow gully lead most parties to carry an ice axe and crampons, and some carry a short rope for the crux step.
bivy: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
current.rope_note: Ridge scramble via Jefferson Creek/Hamma Hamma approach: solid Class 3 with a 'spicy' exposed traverse, and a 4th-class scramble section on a very exposed ridge that confident parties walk unroped. Rock quality is inconsistent.

name: The Hexorcist
beta: Known only as a difficult alpine rock climb by Bryan Burdo on Persis's north face — no detailed grade, pitch count, or topo is available. This is a serious, low-traffic line distinct from the peak's Class 2 West Ridge hiking route; treat it as an alpine rock objective requiring full trad rack, rope, and North Cascades route-finding/approach skills rather than a hiking route.
overview: A difficult, multi-pitch technical alpine rock climb up Mount Persis's sheer north face, established by prolific North Cascades first-ascentionist Bryan Burdo.

current.approach: No maintained trail reaches the north face. Parties generally leave the West Ridge boot path or approach cross-country from the Anderson Creek drainage / FR 6220 area, bushwhacking through steep second-growth and old-growth timber to gain the base of the wall; expect substantial off-trail forest travel and real route-finding difficulty.
current.descent: Not documented for this specific route; likely descends via the peak's easier west-ridge/back-side terrain, as is typical for north-face routes on this peak, but this is not confirmed anywhere.
current.pro_needs: No published topo or rack beta exists for this route; parties should plan for a full, versatile traditional rack given the total absence of documented protection information.

name: Mount Pilchuck Trail (Standard Route)
beta: From the FR 42 trailhead the trail climbs through subalpine forest, crosses open talus/boulder slopes marked with orange blazes below the final headwall, and finishes with roughly 20-30 ft of boulder scrambling and a short fixed steel ladder (rungs can spin underfoot) up to the lookout deck. The route is non-technical hiking/scrambling in dry summer conditions but becomes a genuine, consequential snow/ice ascent whenever the upper mountain still holds snow, which in a heavy year can persist into July.
overview: The Mount Pilchuck Trail (USFS Trail #700) is the standard, and essentially only maintained, route to the summit: a short, steep old-growth-forest and heather-meadow trail that ends with a boulder-field crossing and a brief hands-on scramble plus short ladder to the historic fire lookout on the rocky summit.

current.approach: From Granite Falls, follow WA-92 east and then the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 10-11 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center. Continue about 1 mile past Verlot, cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River, and turn right (south) onto Mount Pilchuck Road (FR 42). Follow FR 42 for about 6.8 miles — rough, washboarded gravel for the first ~4.7 miles and paved for the last ~1.9, with the gravel's condition varying by year — to the Mount Pilchuck Trailhead parking area (roughly 3,000-3,100 ft). In years when FR 42 is gated below the trailhead (common in shoulder season), the hike instead starts from the Heather Lake Trailhead, adding roughly 5 miles and substantial elevation gain each way.
approach_variant_names: Mount Pilchuck Road to the trailhead
From the Heather Lake trailhead when the road is gated
current.descent: From the lookout, reverse the short ladder and boulder-field scramble, then follow the marked trail (orange blazes across the open boulder field, then single-track through forest) back down to the trailhead parking area. Do not attempt to shortcut down the old ski-area clearing visible west of the trail — it looks like a shortcut but is steep and brushy, and has contributed to lost-hiker rescues.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack needed for the standard summer trail — it is a non-technical hike with a class 2-3 boulder scramble at the top.
current.pro_needs: No protection/pro needed in dry conditions; the only real technical consideration is footing on wet or icy granite in the boulder field and on the final scramble/ladder to the lookout.

name: Hester Lake Route
beta: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, follow the Dingford Creek Trail (multiple creek crossings) toward Hester Lake and Little Hester Lake — roughly the first 5-6 miles. From the lakes basin, ascend the boulder field south of Little Hester Lake to gain Price's east ridge near Point 5,480'/5,440', traverse the steep north side of the ridge to a col around 5,400 ft just east of the true summit, and finish with a short ridge scramble to the 5,587 ft summit. Expect Class 3 scrambling with occasional steep snow or rock gullies on the ridge, and real routefinding difficulty — at least one party's own GPS track diverged noticeably between ascent and descent.
overview: A longer wilderness approach up Mount Price's south/east side via the Hester Lake basin, gaining the peak's east ridge by a boulder-field scramble and finishing along a steep, partly snow-and-rock ridge to the summit.

current.approach: Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,400 ft). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail, crossing several creeks, toward the Hester Lake basin (roughly 5-6 miles) before leaving the trail to begin the off-trail scramble.
current.descent: From the summit, reverse the final ridge scramble to the ~5,400 ft col, traverse back across the steep north side of the east ridge, and downclimb the boulder field to the Hester Lake / Little Hester Lake basin. Pick up the Dingford Creek Trail near the lakes and follow it back to the trailhead. Expect brush, including devil's club, below about 4,000 ft when the route is snow-free; allow extra time — one documented trip took over 10 hours car-to-car.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed protection; a rope/light rack could be carried by less experienced parties for the steeper ridge sections, though most parties scramble it unroped.
current.pro_needs: None fixed — unroped scramble; steep snow sections may warrant an axe and, in early season, crampons/microspikes.
bivy: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek

name: Northwest Route
beta: Four cliff bands cross the way, near 2,800, 3,200, 3,600 and 4,500 ft; each goes with careful map reading, and the slopes between are talus or forest. Keep east of the creek draining Price Lake. In snow the gully above the lake is wide and steady. Roughly 4,100 ft of gain over about 4 miles, 4 to 6 hours up. Inside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

current.approach: Take the Dingford Creek trail about 2.2 miles to its crossing of Goat Creek (about 2,600 ft). Leave the trail, cross the valley southward, and enter the basin that holds Price Lake.

name: Southeast Route
beta: Follow the spur through forest to about 4,400 ft, where the trees give way to an open talus slope. Climb the talus, or its edge, to the east-west crest near 5,100 ft, then turn west along the crest, staying on its forested north side because the south face is cliffy. Expect rock steps and towers to be passed or skirted, with hands needed in places. Route-finding is the main challenge. About 3,700 ft of gain and 2 to 3 miles off-trail beyond the road walk, which adds about 8 miles round trip; allow 3 to 5 hours up from the spur. The line stays outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

current.approach: Walk or bike the closed continuation of the Middle Fork road east from the Dingford Creek trailhead for about 4 miles, to the short side road to the hot-springs parking area at roughly 1,800 ft. Leave the road there and head north, bending north-northwest onto the north-south spur ridge that rises from it.

name: South Ridge / Southeast Ridge
beta: From a camp near Thirtynine Mile Creek/Thirtynine Mile Lake, parties push through brush alongside the creek to a relatively brush-free rib and climb to the south ridge crest around 6,600 ft. From there the route follows the ridgeline north over Pt. 6690, Pt. 7361, and the false summit at Pt. 7547 before finishing west to the true summit (7,640+ ft on USGS maps; 7,673 ft per modern LIDAR). Crestline travel is Class 1-2; the false summit and true summit involve steeper Class 3 rock with moderate exposure. Best done mid-to-late summer once the upper southwest cirque's talus/scree has melted out.
overview: Mount Prophet is a heavily forested, remote summit west of Ross Lake inside North Cascades National Park — Washington's 18th-most-prominent peak. The standard route is a long, brushy multi-day approach up Big Beaver Trail followed by a Class 2-3 scramble along the south/southeast ridge crest, with a short Class 3 step near the summit.

current.approach: From Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20, MP 134) hike the Ross Lake shoreline trail ~7 mi to the Big Beaver Trail junction (or take the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing to shorten this), then continue ~5 mi up Big Beaver Trail to Thirtynine Mile Creek/Camp. Leave the trail there and climb a brushy forested rib to gain the south ridge at a ~6,600 ft saddle. Round trip from the Big Beaver Landing water-taxi drop is roughly 18 miles with 7,000+ ft of elevation gain, typically done over 2-3 days; walking the lakeshore both ways instead adds about 14 miles. From the saddle, follow the ridge crest (Class 1-2) past points 7,361 ft and 7,547 ft to a short Class 3 step below the true summit; Luna Camp, about 5 miles farther up Big Beaver Trail, is the start of the separate Southwest Rib route, not this one.
approach_variant_names: Big Beaver valley to Thirtynine Mile Creek, then the ridge
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: follow the ridge crest back down past the two intermediate high points, with the short Class 3 step below the summit taken carefully on the way down, to the saddle around 6,600 ft. Drop the brushy forested rib to Thirtynine Mile Creek, the last reliable water, and rejoin Big Beaver Trail. From there it is about 5 miles of trail back toward Ross Lake, and the lakeshore trail or the water taxi from Big Beaver Landing completes the exit. Loose rock on the upper ridge is a rockfall hazard for anyone below you, and the brush on the rib is slow in the dark.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is typically needed on the standard South/Southeast Ridge line — it is a scramble, not a roped climb. Some parties carry a short rope and a few slings/runners to belay less-experienced members through the exposed Class 3 moves near the false and true summits.
rack: Rope + 1-2 snow pickets (optional, early-season south ridge snow or a Southwest Rib descent)
current.pro_needs: No technical rack needed for the standard Class 2-3 ridge line; a rope with one or two snow pickets is worth carrying early season for the south ridge snow, or if planning a Southwest Rib descent through its ~6,900 ft cliff-band snow ramp.
current.rope_note: South Ridge/Southeast Ridge route (via Thirtynine Mile Creek) is mostly Class 1-2 ridge travel with short Class 3 rock sections near the false and true summits; exposure is explicitly described as 'never bad.' Rope not required for competent parties.

name: Southwest Rib
beta: From Luna Camp, ford the creek and climb through brush that eases quickly, keeping the main creek on the left, until around 3,800 ft where the slope narrows into a forested rib with easy travel. At about 5,450 ft the route traverses southeast to a wall, descends 5-10 ft onto a downward-sloping ledge past two short Class 4 chimneys and a few arêtes (the technical crux, only about 10-15 vertical feet of Class 4), then continues into the southwest cirque. A cliff band at the top of the cirque (~6,900 ft) is bypassed via a snow ramp on its far right (east) side, leading to a saddle east of the peak at ~7,420 ft. From there the route follows the summit ridge, passing a gendarme on its south side, to the true summit.
overview: The other standard line up Mount Prophet: a forested rib climbed from the Big Beaver/Luna Camp basin, through a short Class 4 chimney crux on a rock wall, then a snow-ramp bypass of a cliff band into the southwest cirque and a ridge finish to the summit. Best done in spring/early summer before cornices form.

current.approach: As for the South/Southeast Ridge: SR-20 to the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134), then the Ross Dam Trail and Big Beaver Trail (or the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing) up the Big Beaver Creek valley to Luna Camp, the base camp for this route.
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: down the summit ridge past the gendarme to the 7,420 ft saddle, down the snow ramp past the 6,900 ft cliff band, back through the Class 4 chimney/ledge section at ~5,450 ft, and down the forested rib to Luna Camp.
current.detailed_rack: Generally climbed as an unroped scramble; some parties carry a short rope, a sling or two, and a small cam for the two short Class 4 chimneys at roughly 5,450 ft.
current.pro_needs: Minimal — protection, if carried, is only for the brief Class 4 chimney/ledge crux.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Mount Pulitzer is reached almost exclusively as part of the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse, an off-trail alpine route through Olympic National Park's interior. From a camp near Lone Tree Pass, climbers head north along faint game/boot paths on open ridge terrain to the Ferry-Pulitzer col, then scramble the East Ridge on class 3 rock to Pulitzer's false summit. Parties describe this stretch as relaxed, scenic scrambling with time to examine wildflowers and quartz crystals in the rock. The true summit, visible from the false summit as an inviting rock horn, requires crossing a horribly shattered sedimentary ridge with serious exposure that has stopped experienced parties; many groups instead traverse over to nearby Mount Ferry (an easier double-summit peak) from the same camp rather than push for Pulitzer's true top.
overview: Mount Pulitzer (also historically called Snagtooth) is the sixth-highest summit in the Bailey Range, about 0.6 mile from Mount Ferry in the Olympic interior. It is a distinct peak from the separate, higher Wellesley Peak elsewhere in the range, despite the two names sometimes being conflated. The standard line follows the east ridge (the 1961 first-ascent route), approached from a high camp in Ferry Basin or at Lone Tree Pass, over heather, snow, and talus. The final scramble to the true summit crosses badly shattered, exposed rock that some parties have judged too loose to finish, opting instead for nearby Mount Ferry. The remote, multi-day Bailey Range approach remains the main challenge.

current.approach: Begins on the High Divide Trail from the Sol Duc Trailhead, leaving maintained trail near the 'Catwalk' below Mount Carrie to join the cross-country Bailey Range traverse. A multi-day approach over rugged, mostly off-trail terrain reaches a high camp below Pulitzer and Mount Ferry (Ferry Basin, or Lone Tree Pass just south of Pulitzer), from which the east ridge is scrambled to the summit.
current.descent: For an out-and-back side trip from Ferry Basin, reverse the east ridge to the Ferry–Pulitzer col and descend to camp. Parties continuing the full Bailey Range Traverse instead push on south off Pulitzer toward Lone Tree Pass and Bear Pass rather than retracing their steps, dropping into Queets Basin en route toward Mount Olympus and the Elwha Snowfinger exit.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed technical rock rack is standard for the East Ridge scramble itself. Because Pulitzer is only reached via the Bailey Range Traverse, parties carry full glacier travel kit for the approach, including a glacier rope for crossing Bailey Range snowfields and glaciers such as the one on Pulitzer's own north slope and Humes Glacier further south.
rack: Small nut set (optional, carried by some parties for the loose, exposed final ridge to the true summit)
Glacier rope + crevasse-rescue hardware (Tibloc/Micro Traxion) for Bailey Range glacier crossings
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed on the standard scramble route; a small nut set has been carried by some parties for the loose, exposed final ridge to the true summit but is not standard gear for most ascents (many parties decline that section entirely).
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found; Class 3 rating is consistent with non-technical Olympic-style scrambling — rope not standard.

name: North Ridge
beta: Mount Queets sits just southwest of the Bailey Range in the interior of Olympic National Park. There is no maintained trail to the summit — reaching it requires a multi-day cross-country wilderness approach, commonly combined with nearby Mount Meany and/or a longer Bailey Range or Queets Basin traverse.
overview: Mount Queets (6,476 ft) is a remote summit in the interior Olympic Mountains, sitting on the divide near the headwaters of both the Elwha and Queets rivers, just southwest of the Bailey Range and Dodwell-Rixon Pass. It is built of Eocene basalt, and heavy winter snowfall sustains the small Queets Glacier in a cirque on its north slope despite the peak's modest elevation. Harry Fisher (recorded as James B. Hanmore) and Nelson Linsley made the first recorded ascent in 1890 during the Army's O'Neil Expedition. There is no maintained trail to the peak; it lies deep in Olympic National Park wilderness and is normally climbed either as a side objective from the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse or via a dedicated cross-country backpack up the Elwha River to Elwha Basin.

current.approach: There is no direct trailhead-to-summit trail. Vehicle access to the Elwha Valley has been closed since a May 2021 washout on Olympic Hot Springs Road; you now walk or bike an extra ~6-7 miles from the Madison Falls parking area (past the washout, then up Whiskey Bend Road) just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead. From Whiskey Bend, follow the Elwha River Trail to Chicago Camp, where it fords the Elwha short of Low Divide, then leave the trail and continue about 3 miles cross-country up into Elwha Basin and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763 ft) to reach the north ridge of Mount Queets. Most parties treat this as a multi-day (4+ day round trip) wilderness objective, commonly combined with the Bailey Range Traverse via Queets Basin to the west. The lower third of the north ridge is mostly 2nd-class scrambling on crumbly rock and heather; where it becomes impassable, drop a few hundred feet to traverse steep, firm scree around 5,300 ft on the east side to bypass a cliff band, then regain the ridge for an easy 2nd-class scramble around its west side before a moderately steep snow slope on the east side leads to the summit. Microspikes and an axe have been used here even in late August.
approach_variant_names: Elwha Basin and Dodwell-Rixon Pass to the north ridge
current.descent: Descend the north ridge, retracing the route over Dodwell-Rixon Pass to the Elwha Basin camp.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble line; the terrain is unroped class 2-3 scrambling with a snow-slope crossing near the top. Less experienced parties sometimes carry a light rope and a picket or two for the snow slope, but most climbers travel unroped throughout.
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and informal: an ice axe (self-arrest) for the summit snow slope is the main 'protection' most parties carry; a rope/picket is optional insurance for less-experienced climbers on that slope only.
bivy: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
current.rope_note: Mount Queets has multiple named routes spanning Class 2 to Class 4; this South Slopes line's Class 3 rating sits mid-range — no rope typically required, though the peak supports a small glacier so early-season parties should watch for snow/ice.

name: Custer-Rahm Traverse
beta: Undertaken as a link between the two peaks (not from a trailhead) after climbing one via another route. Rahm-to-Custer is the easier direction to routefind: follow the crest (exposed on the north side, easier scrambling on flatter rock) to a notch below Custer's final arête, then find a hidden Class 4 gully roughly 50 ft below and left of the notch to bypass the unfeasible Class 5 arête. Custer-to-Rahm is the harder direction to routefind, since the crux gully is difficult to spot from above.
overview: A high, mostly Class 2/3 ridge-crest traverse directly connecting the summits of Mount Rahm and Mount Custer, with one short Class 4 gully bypassing an unclimbable arête near Custer's summit block.

current.approach: Reached from the summit of either Mount Rahm (via the Standard Route/Glacier or South Side) or Mount Custer (via its South Ridge), not from a trailhead directly.
current.descent: Parties doing this traverse essentially never reverse it. From Custer's summit, descend the South Ridge route back toward Ouzel Lake or the Depot Creek-Silver Lake saddle camp; from Rahm's summit, descend the South Side route's gully system back to camp.
current.detailed_rack: Light and fast: carry a 30m rope and a few slings only as a rappel option if descending the harder (Custer-to-Rahm) direction, since the gully's anchor quality is reportedly poor and untested.
current.pro_needs: Minimal — this is an unroped scramble except for a possible short rappel of the Class 4 crux gully when traveling Custer-to-Rahm.
bivy: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek

name: South Side
beta: From camp, ascend cross-country to an upper terrace below the Custer-Rahm ridge, then locate a narrow, oblique gully cutting through a roughly 100-ft cliff band — it's hidden until you're right on it, at an inside corner of the cliff. Climb the gully's right-hand fork through its short crux (the left fork dead-ends in a loose, walled amphitheater), then continue up talus/scree and a moderate-angle snowfield in the upper basin to the south spur and the east summit; the west summit, a short ridge walk away, carries the higher mapped contour.
overview: A talus, gully, and snowfield scramble that gains Mount Rahm's summit from the south via Ouzel Lake or Silver Lake camp, with the only real obstacle being a short Class 4/5 gully through a cliff band at 7,700 ft.

current.approach: Two camps are used: Silver Lake (6,763 ft, reached via a long Silver Creek bushwhack from Ross Lake) or Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft, reached via the Depot Creek approach from Chilliwack Lake Road, BC — the easier of the two to reach). From Ouzel Lake, climb northeast up an obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle, then traverse and ascend southwestward below the Custer-Rahm ridge to the roughly 7,400-ft upper terrace. From Silver Lake, climb above the lakeside cliffs to the northwest, or walk the north shore west until the cliffs end, then climb talus/slabs north to the same terrace.
approach_variant_names: Depot Creek from the Canadian side
Silver Creek from Ross Lake
current.descent: No rappel anchors are reported in the crux gully; downclimb it (the alternate, longer Class 3 gully just downhill and right of it may be an easier downclimb than the Class 4/5 line). From the upper terrace, reverse the traverse back down to the Custer-Spickard saddle and Ouzel Lake camp, or to Silver Lake, or continue over to Mount Custer if adding it to the day.
current.detailed_rack: No rack is needed for protection — this is an unroped scramble.
current.pro_needs: None — the crux gully is short (about 40 ft) and typically climbed without protection; a helmet is the main safety item.

name: Curtis Ridge
beta: Considered technically harder, more confusing, and more committing than Liberty Ridge or Ptarmigan Ridge; a solid Grade IV climb with roughly 7,000 vertical ft of climbing, with a key rappel and 4th-class scrambling through rock bands.
overview: A long, serious ridge separating the Carbon and Winthrop Glaciers on Rainier's north side, running directly alongside the infamous Willis Wall. From White River Campground, climbers hike to Glacier Basin, ascend to St. Elmo Pass, then descend onto the Winthrop Glacier (crossing it between roughly 7,300-7,400 ft) to reach the base of the ridge.

current.approach: From White River Campground (reached via WA-410 and White River Road — check the park's current road status for early/late-season openings), hike the Glacier Basin Trail roughly 3.5 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Glacier Basin (~5,900 ft), a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camping spot. From there, continue on climbers' path up to St. Elmo Pass (~7,400 ft), gaining another ~1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree/snow. At St. Elmo Pass, rope up for glacier travel: drop down onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west/southwest, threading around crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east (Winthrop) side. This is the same approach corridor used for Liberty Ridge, so expect other parties and established boot tracks in season. Above St. Elmo Pass there is no water; carry enough for the climb or plan to melt snow.
approach_variant_names: White River, Glacier Basin, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier traverse
current.descent: Curtis Ridge tops out onto the upper mountain near the Winthrop/Emmons basin, and the standard descent is to continue over the summit area and down the Emmons-Winthrop Glacier route to Camp Schurman, then follow the established boot path down the Inter Glacier back toward Glacier Basin and out to White River. This is a walk-off/glissade descent, not a rappel descent — many parties glissade a substantial chunk (roughly 2,000-3,000 vertical feet) of the Inter Glacier snowfield above Glacier Basin when conditions allow, which is the fastest way off the mountain on this side. No fixed rappels are used; standard crevasse-rescue gear covers the glacier sections.
current.detailed_rack: Technical alpine rack: two tools, ice screws, pickets, a light rock rack for mixed steps, a single rope, full crevasse-rescue kit.
rack: Two ice tools, ice screws, pickets
current.pro_needs: Ice screws, pickets, and a light rock rack for mixed sections
current.rope_note: Single 60m rope for glacier travel plus short rappels off the ridge crest; carry extra cord to leave at rappel anchors in case existing tat looks bad.

name: Edmunds Headwall
beta: First skied in 1997 by Armond DuBuque, Doug Ingersoll, Andrew McLean, and Carl Skoog; historically accessed via the Mowich Lake road, which has had no public access since the SR 165 bridge closed in April 2025.
overview: A sustained, direct line dropping off Liberty Cap on Rainier's northwest side, from roughly 13,400' to 9,900'; first climbed in 1957 as the earliest line up the Mowich side, a snow and ice climb to Liberty Cap.

current.approach: From Mowich Lake, hike through Spray Park and up the lower Ptarmigan Ridge to camps near 9,600 ft between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers, then drop to the Edmunds Glacier and the base of the headwall.
approach_variant_names: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the 9,600 ft divide, then across to the Edmunds Glacier
current.descent: From Liberty Cap descend toward the summit and the Emmons-Winthrop Glacier to Camp Schurman and White River, or descend west-side glaciers toward Mowich; plan exit logistics.
current.detailed_rack: Technical alpine kit: two tools, ice screws, pickets, a single rope for simul/belays, full crevasse-rescue gear.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets on the steep face; simul-climbing on moderate terrain.
